summary: Reviewed 3 files: HttpToolDownloader.cs, HttpToolDownloaderTests.cs, FfmpegProvisionerLiveTests.cs. 0 Critical, 0 High, 0 Medium. 2 Low/Info observations recorded. Security sign-off: PASS.

comments.note: A03/A09 — URL logged as structured parameter: HttpToolDownloader.cs lines 51-54 log `url` and `destinationPath` via `_logger.LogInformation(...)`. Structured logging (Serilog) serializes these as separate fields, preventing log injection. No current risk — all URLs are manifest entries from appsettings.json with no embedded credentials. Defence-in-depth: if URLs ever gain query-string auth tokens (e.g., SAS tokens, signed URLs), they would appear in log sinks. Recommendation: if that pattern is adopted in future, redact or hash the URL query string before logging.

A10 — No URL scheme/domain allowlist in DownloadAsync (HttpToolDownloader.cs line 38): `url` is passed directly to `HttpClient.GetAsync` without validation of scheme or host. Currently fully mitigated — all callers supply manifest URLs from application-controlled appsettings.json. No SSRF exposure exists in the current call graph. Defence-in-depth recommendation: consider a guard that rejects non-HTTPS schemes or URLs not matching expected CDN domains (e.g., `github.com`, `johnvansickle.com`) to harden against a future path where `url` originates from less-trusted input.

No additional security findings. All OWASP Top 10 categories reviewed. A01 (access control): destination path is application-controlled, no user-supplied path input. A02 (crypto): SHA-256 verification handled by Sha256ChecksumVerifier (out of scope). A04 (insecure design): temp-then-atomic-move pattern is sound; cancellation correctly removes the partial temp file. A05 (misconfiguration): no hardcoded credentials, no verbose error disclosure to callers (exceptions re-thrown as-is). A06 (outdated components): no new dependencies introduced. A07/A08: not applicable to this download utility.

summary: Reviewed 3 files: HttpToolDownloader.cs, HttpToolDownloaderTests.cs, FfmpegProvisionerLiveTests.cs. No blocking issues found. One Fix-Forward applied: OperationCanceledException in the catch block was logged at LogError, which would pollute error dashboards with user-initiated cancellations; changed to LogInformation (non-behavioral — tests do not validate log levels). Build and 63 Infrastructure tests re-verified green post-fix. All 5 acceptance criteria confirmed met.

comments.note: HttpToolDownloader.cs catch block: OperationCanceledException was logged at LogError, which would cause user/timeout-initiated cancellations to appear in error monitoring dashboards (false positives). Applied Fix-Forward: added an if/else branch — OperationCanceledException now logs at LogInformation with a 'Download cancelled' message; all other exceptions retain LogError. Non-behavioral change: program control flow, temp file cleanup, and re-throw are unchanged. 63 tests green post-fix.

HttpToolDownloader.cs: the Stopwatch is started AFTER EnsureSuccessStatusCode() and the 'Download starting' log. ElapsedMs in the success log therefore measures only the streaming/file-write phase, not the full HTTP round-trip including response-header retrieval. This is acceptable for its intended purpose (I/O timing) but is worth understanding if the metric is ever surfaced in a dashboard — the label 'Download succeeded ... ElapsedMs' could be misread as end-to-end latency.

HttpToolDownloader.cs: File.Move(tempPath, destinationPath, overwrite: true) is called outside the try/catch block. If File.Move throws (e.g., cross-device rename not supported, or insufficient permissions at destination), the .tmp file is orphaned on disk. Current risk is low — same-volume moves are atomic on Windows/Linux — but consider wrapping File.Move in a try/finally that cleans up tempPath if promotion fails.

[documentation-forward] HttpToolDownloader.DownloadAsync: the XML doc on the method should mention that ElapsedMs in the success log measures the streaming/file-write phase only (not the full HTTP round-trip). Additionally, the class-level summary could note the ILogger<HttpToolDownloader> constructor parameter and what log events it emits (start, success, failure, cancellation) so consumers know what to expect in their log sinks.
